paragraphs: The small, rain-slick streets of Blackthorn Hollow were eerily quiet as Detective Eleanor Vance arrived at the scene. The old Windsor mansion loomed before her, its gothic spires cutting into the foggy night sky. Inside, a murder had been reported—Victor Pembroke, the reclusive millionaire and owner of the estate, was found dead in his study. His assistant, Clara Finch, trembling and pale, had made the frantic call to the police. As Eleanor stepped into the grand but shadowed foyer, she found three other figures assembled: Marianne Pembroke, Victor’s enigmatic niece; Harold Gaines, a business partner with a faltering frown; and Richard Lyle, the brooding groundskeeper who seemed to belong to the shadows themselves. Each pair of eyes told its own story, yet each was undeniably haunted by the revelation of Victor's violent end.

Eleanor wasted no time in addressing the group, her sharp gaze moving from one face to the next. “Victor Pembroke didn’t just fall over dead,” she said firmly, her voice cutting through the thick silence. “Someone in this house had a motive, and someone in this house carried it out.” Clara Finch, the assistant, was the first to speak, her voice shaking. “I-I only found him. He was slumped over his desk. The letter opener—there was blood everywhere.” At this, Richard Lyle, the groundskeeper, gave a low, unsettling chuckle. “Rich men like him always end up on the wrong side of someone’s temper. No one cries for a man like Victor Pembroke.” Harold Gaines shot him a sharp look, his jaw tightening. “Have some respect, will you? Victor was difficult, yes, but he didn’t deserve this.” Marianne Pembroke, the niece, remained silent in the corner, her dark eyes fixed on something distant, her expression unreadable. Eleanor noticed her hands were trembling slightly. “Well,” Eleanor murmured, “Everyone has something they’re not saying. Let’s find out what.”

Eleanor moved to the study where Victor’s body had been discovered. The air was thick with the smell of dried blood and polished oak. The millionaire’s lifeless form still slumped over the desk, just as Clara had described. The letter opener—a silver, monogrammed implement—was embedded in his chest, the handle smeared crimson. She noted the precision of the stabbing; it wasn’t haphazard, as if someone had been in a blind rage. This attack was calculated. Her eyes scanned the room, settling on a torn piece of paper gripped tightly in Victor’s right hand. Carefully, she pried it free, revealing part of a sentence: “...cannot protect you any longer.” It was written in a hasty scrawl. “Protect who from what?” Eleanor muttered under her breath. As she pocketed the fragment, she noticed Harold Gaines standing in the doorway, his arms crossed tightly. “Did you find what you were looking for, Detective?” he asked, his voice too casual. Eleanor turned to face him, feeling a flicker of suspicion at his composure. "We’ll see," she replied, noting how his eyes briefly darted to the letter opener, then back to her.

Eleanor left the study and found Richard Lyle lingering near the library, his rough hands fiddling with a stray thread on his fraying coat. “You've got questions, don’t you?” he muttered before she could even approach. His voice was low, almost guttural, like someone accustomed to keeping secrets. “You worked closely with Victor, didn’t you?” Eleanor asked evenly. Richard snorted, shaking his head. “Worked *under* him, more like. He liked to act like he owned the whole damn world, including the people in it.” The bitterness in his tone was unmistakable. “So, you’re saying you didn’t get along?” Eleanor pressed, watching his eyes narrow. “I’m saying he didn’t get along with anyone,” Richard shot back. "He treated me like dirt, same as he treated her." He flicked his gaze towards Marianne, who was sitting stiffly in the corner of the foyer. “Don’t let her innocent act fool you. She’s got more venom in her than a snake.” Eleanor raised an eyebrow but said nothing, letting his words hang in the air. Richard smirked darkly before heading toward the door, his boots echoing loudly on the polished floor.

Eleanor redirected her attention to Marianne, who still sat motionless in the corner, her gaze fixed on the rain beating against the window. “Miss Pembroke,” Eleanor began, carefully approaching her. Marianne flinched slightly, as though pulled from a trance. “You’ve been quiet all evening. Care to tell me where you were when your uncle was murdered?” Marianne’s lips parted, but it took her a moment to speak. “In my room,” she said softly, her voice barely audible. “I... I didn’t hear anything. He always kept the study locked when he didn’t want to be disturbed.” Eleanor tilted her head, doubting the claim. “Your hands are trembling, Marianne. Are you frightened—or hiding something?” Marianne’s eyes flashed angrily as she shot back, “You think I’d kill the only family I have left? He may not have been kind, but he... he took care of me.” Her voice cracked slightly, and she looked away. Eleanor noticed the faint scent of cigar smoke on her clothes, strange for someone who claimed to have been upstairs the entire time. “Odd,” Eleanor mused aloud, “your story doesn’t match the scent clinging to you. Did you stop by the study earlier?” Marianne clenched her jaw and stood abruptly, but before she could reply, Clara Finch appeared in the doorway with wide, startled eyes. “Detective, I’ve found something you need to see,” Clara stammered, clutching a small black notebook tightly to her chest.

The notebook was old and worn, the leather cover cracked at the edges from years of use. Clara handed it to Eleanor with trembling hands. “I found it in Mr. Pembroke’s desk drawer while trying to sort through the mess,” she explained quickly. Eleanor flipped it open, scanning the pages. Most were filled with what seemed to be financial notes and scattered musings, but one entry near the end caught her eye. The handwriting was frantic, almost desperate: *“I’ve been threatened again. If I don't hand it over, they’ll destroy everything I’ve built. But how can I trust any of them? Marianne is restless, Harold grows impatient, and Richard... God help me if Richard learns the truth.”* Eleanor’s heart quickened, her mind turning over the implications. “You read this?” she asked Clara, glancing up sharply. The assistant shook her head quickly, her pale face betraying her fear. “No, no, I swear. I didn’t read anything... I was just organizing...” Eleanor closed the notebook slowly, her eyes narrowing as she flicked a glance at Harold, who had just stepped into the room. He was watching her carefully, his lips pressed into a thin line. She noticed the tension in his shoulders as he caught sight of the notebook. “Everything all right, Detective?” Harold asked, a little too smoothly. Eleanor tucked the notebook under her arm. “Quite,” she replied, but something about his formality felt forced.

Eleanor decided to confront Harold directly, curious to test his reaction. “Mr. Gaines,” she began, motioning for him to follow her into the quiet sitting room adjacent to the foyer. He hesitated but complied, his hands clasped firmly behind his back. Once they were alone, she turned to him, withdrawing the notebook and holding it up like an accusation. “Victor seemed to think you were growing ‘impatient.’ Care to explain?” Harold’s face twitched almost imperceptibly, but he quickly masked it with a polite smile. “Victor and I had a long history, Detective. Business partnerships are rarely without frustrations. What did he expect, sitting on a deal that would have benefited us both?” Eleanor’s eyes narrowed. “What deal? I wasn’t aware of any ongoing business ventures.” Harold took a step closer, lowering his voice. “Victor didn’t mention it because he was stalling. We were negotiating the sale of one of his properties—a piece of land that I’ve been trying to acquire for years. He kept raising the price, playing games, trying to squeeze me for more.” His bitterness was hard to miss. “And did you meet with Victor tonight? Perhaps to settle more than just the price?” Eleanor asked, her tone sharper. Harold stiffened, his forced calm beginning to crack. “I had words with him earlier,” he admitted. “But he was alive when I walked out of that study.” Eleanor noted the way his knuckles whitened against his palms. “You should be careful with assumptions, Detective,” he added darkly, before turning on his heel and leaving the room.

As Harold disappeared down the hall, Eleanor stood still for a moment, her mind calculating. She pocketed the notebook and made her way back to the foyer, where Clara was now nervously wringing her hands near the grand staircase. “Miss Finch,” Eleanor called, and Clara jumped as though caught doing something wrong. “I need you to tell me exactly what you saw when you found Victor’s body.” Clara swallowed hard, glancing nervously at the study door. “I had gone to deliver a stack of papers he asked for earlier… but when I knocked, he didn’t answer. The door was unlocked, so I pushed it open, and that’s when I saw him, slumped over the desk with… with the letter opener.” Her voice cracked at the memory. “I screamed. I didn’t mean to, but it just… I ran out and called the police.” Eleanor studied Clara’s trembling form. “Did anyone else come into the study before the police arrived?” Clara hesitated, her eyes darting toward the staircase. “I… I don’t think so. I can’t be sure. I wasn’t paying attention.” Eleanor frowned, sensing there was more Clara wasn’t saying. “You’re certain the door was unlocked when you entered?” Clara nodded quickly. “Yes, I swear! But Mr. Pembroke never left it unlocked unless he—unless someone else was with him earlier.” The statement hung in the air like a shadow, and Eleanor stored the detail away. “I’ll need you to stay close,” she instructed firmly, though her gaze briefly flitted toward the staircase Clara kept glancing at, wondering what, or who, might still be lurking.

Eleanor’s curiosity about the staircase grew stronger, so she ascended carefully, her boots whispering against the plush, wine-red carpet. At the top, the narrow hallway split into two wings, dimly lit by flickering sconces. She noticed Marianne’s door slightly ajar to her right. The faint scent of cigar smoke, which she’d detected on Marianne earlier, lingered stronger here, curling faintly into the air. She pushed the door open fully to find Marianne’s room neat but not overly so—cluttered books on philosophy and psychology were stacked on the desk, and an open trunk at the foot of the bed revealed layers of disheveled clothing. On the nightstand lay a crystal ashtray with the dark, spent stub of a cigar resting atop its edge. Eleanor picked it up gently, inspecting the brand. It matched the box of cigars sitting prominently on Victor’s desk downstairs. She frowned; the connection was subtle but unmistakable. Marianne stood suddenly in the doorway behind her, her face pale, her arms crossed. “Is this an official search?” she asked, her tone sharp. “Victor gave me one from his collection earlier,” she added defensively before Eleanor could even respond. “It’s not a crime to smoke.” The detective raised an eyebrow, not moving from her spot. “Earlier? When exactly?” Marianne hesitated, the fight slowly draining from her posture. “I—I don’t remember. We spoke briefly… this afternoon.” The vague reply hung in the air, and Eleanor studied her carefully. “What were you talking about?” she pressed. Marianne blinked, her voice faltering. “It doesn’t matter anymore, does it? He’s dead.” She stepped back from the door, pulling it shut with quiet force. The lock clicked, leaving Eleanor with the heavy scent of suspicion.

Descending the stairs once more, Eleanor’s mind spun as she tried to piece together the fragments of motive and opportunity hovering over each suspect. As her boots touched the hardwood of the foyer again, Richard Lyle leaned casually against the wall near the grand clock, his dark eyes tracking her movements like a predator watching prey. “Find something interesting snooping around upstairs, Detective?” he asked, a wolfish grin tugging at the corner of his mouth. Eleanor crossed her arms and met his gaze with steady calm. “You seem awfully relaxed while the rest of the house trembles, Mr. Lyle. Care to explain that confidence?” Richard chuckled, his voice a low rumble. “Unlike some people here, I don’t have anything to hide.” His calm demeanor only served to make Eleanor more cautious. “And where were you during the time of the murder?” she asked pointedly. Without hesitation, Richard replied, “Out back in the garden. You can check my gloves in the shed if you don’t believe me—they’re still covered in soil.” He leaned in slightly, his voice dropping. “But you don’t seem too interested in those types of details, now, do you? You’re heading for the wrong target. I told you before—Marianne’s the one you should watch. She’s playing innocent, but she’s got more backbone than she lets on. Uncle Victor probably crossed the line with her once too often.” He grinned again, almost enjoying the drama. Eleanor said nothing, filing his words away. She knew better than to let his swagger steer her too fully. She finally broke his gaze and turned toward the study yet again. Something didn’t add up, and it was beginning to smell deliberate.

Eleanor re-entered the study, her sharp eyes combing over the space with fresh determination. The room seemed almost too pristine aside from the gruesome scene at the desk—every book on the mahogany shelf was aligned perfectly, the cigar box on the desk almost ceremoniously placed, the decanter of whiskey untouched. But then, as she traced Victor’s desk with her gloved fingers, something caught her attention: an empty spot in the fine layer of dust lining the back corner of the desk. It was faint, but the rectangular imprint suggested that something small and flat had been removed recently. A photograph, perhaps? Or a document? Her thoughts were interrupted by Clara Finch, who had timidly entered the study behind her. “Detective, I—I wanted to mention something. About earlier.” Eleanor turned to face her slowly, narrowing her eyes. “What is it, Miss Finch?” Clara hesitated, clutching the hem of her cardigan. “I didn’t want to say it in front of the others, but… when I ran out of this room—after I found him—I thought I saw someone near the back entrance. It was dark, and I wasn’t paying attention, but I’m certain someone was there.” Eleanor stepped toward her, noting the genuine fear in Clara’s expression. “Did you see who it was?” she pressed. Clara’s voice dipped to a near whisper. “I—I think it may have been Richard.” The words dripped with reluctance, as though she were unsure whether even she believed them completely. Eleanor’s lips thinned. If Clara was right, it made Richard’s alibi about working in the garden tenuous at best. But something about her claim lingered unnervingly in the back of Eleanor’s mind—just enough doubt to keep things murky.

Leaving the study once more, Eleanor sought out Richard in the hopes of confronting him about Clara’s claim. She found him outside the back entrance, leaning against the cold, ivy-covered stone wall with a cigarette burning lazily between his fingers. The thick scent of smoke and wet earth hung in the air. “Detective,” he greeted, exhaling a plume of smoke that seemed to swirl with his words. “Come to accuse me of something else?” Eleanor crossed her arms. “Clara says she saw someone near this door right after she discovered Victor’s body. She thinks it was you. Care to explain?” Richard chuckled, a sound both low and menacing. “Clara?” he repeated, dragging out her name with disdain. “She’s always worked herself into a frenzy over nothing. Probably imagined it. I already told you where I was—out in the garden, not skulking around some back door.” Eleanor’s gaze never wavered. “Garden work at night? Convenient.” He shrugged, unbothered. “Plants don’t wait for perfect timing, Detective.” As his grin widened, her eyes were drawn to something peculiar—an unmistakable smudge of dirt on the edge of the back doorknob. Fresh dirt, damp and dark. “What’s that then, Richard?” she asked, pointing toward it. His expression faltered ever so briefly before he snuffed out his cigarette against the wall. “I went through that door earlier in the evening,” he admitted, though no trace of guilt colored his tone. “Had to grab a tool from the shed. What are you implying exactly?” Eleanor held her silence, growing ever more aware of how easily suspicion could align against Richard. But the timing gnawed at her, as did the ease with which he explained it away. Nothing about this man seemed straightforward—except, perhaps, how suspicious he wanted to appear.

Eleanor left Richard to his smirking defiance, her thoughts swirling with threads of doubt that refused to weave into a coherent picture. As she stepped back inside the mansion, she nearly bumped into Marianne, who was pacing the foyer, her arms hugging her chest. “Detective,” Marianne said, her voice sharp yet brittle, “I need to talk to you.” Eleanor paused, studying the younger woman carefully. “Go on,” she urged. Marianne glanced around, her expression guarded. “I… I overheard something earlier tonight. Something between Uncle Victor and Harold. They were arguing in the study. Loud enough that I could hear it from the hallway.” Her words tumbled out quickly, as though she had been holding them back far too long. “What were they arguing about?” Eleanor asked, folding her arms. Marianne shifted uneasily. “Uncle said something about betraying trust. About Harold pushing him too far. I couldn’t make out everything, but…” She hesitated, biting her lip. “They sounded like they were talking about money. Or land. Something important.” Her hands gripped her elbows tighter. “Harold stormed out not long after. That was the last time I saw Uncle alive.” Eleanor locked eyes with her, sensing both urgency and a touch of something darker in Marianne's tone. “And you’re just now telling me this?” she asked, raising a brow. Marianne scowled. “I didn’t realize you’d waste time questioning me while the real threat walks free.” Eleanor noted the venom in her words and the deliberate shift of blame toward Harold. “Thank you, Marianne,” she said calmly, but the feeling that Marianne was trying too hard to divert suspicion refused to leave her mind. No one here was as transparent as they seemed.

Eleanor found Harold in the sitting room, seated stiffly in a leather armchair with a glass of brandy in hand. He didn’t look up as she entered, instead swirling the amber liquid absentmindedly, lost in thought. “You and Victor argued earlier today,” Eleanor stated bluntly, watching him closely. Harold’s grip on the glass tightened, but he didn’t deny it. “Yes, we argued,” he admitted, his voice low and measured. He finally raised his eyes to meet hers, a flicker of resentment sparking behind them. “Victor had a way of pushing people’s limits. He was impossible to negotiate with.” Eleanor stepped closer, her boots clicking softly against the hardwood. “What were you negotiating, exactly? Marianne said she overheard you two—something about trust and money.” Harold’s jaw tightened, and he set the glass down on the side table with more force than necessary. “It was business,” he snapped. “Victor owed me—owed a lot of people, frankly—but he refused to honor his commitments. For someone so wealthy, he was a stingy old bastard. He thought he was untouchable.” Harold rubbed his temples as if the memory alone pained him. “I told him I wouldn’t tolerate it anymore. I left to cool off. And now he's dead.” Eleanor tilted her head. “Convenient timing, isn’t it?” Harold shot her a sharp look, his composure cracking an inch. “If you think I killed him, you’re mistaken. He was alive when I left, Detective. I might’ve wanted my due, but I’m not a murderer.” His words sounded rehearsed, too calculated to be entirely natural. Eleanor let the silence stretch, the weight of his defensiveness thick in the room. Finally, she turned away, but not before noting the faint trace of sweat glistening on Harold’s brow.

As Eleanor left Harold to stew in his own tension, she found Clara hovering anxiously near the base of the staircase, her eyes darting nervously between Eleanor and the study door down the hall. “Detective,” Clara began, her voice hesitant, “I… I think there’s something else I should tell you.” Eleanor stopped mid-step, crossing her arms and fixing Clara with a steady gaze. “Go on.” The young assistant hesitated, chewing her lip as she glanced around to confirm no one else was within earshot. “Mr. Pembroke and Harold weren’t the only ones fighting,” she said quietly. “Earlier today, Mr. Pembroke and Miss Marianne had a terrible row. I heard it from the hallway outside the study. She was yelling about wanting to leave, about him controlling her life. He told her that if she left, she’d lose everything—no money, no home, nothing. She stormed out afterward, and he slammed the door so hard the whole house shook.” Eleanor’s eyes narrowed. “Why didn’t you mention this before?” she asked sharply. Clara looked down, guilt coloring her face. “I didn’t think… I mean, Marianne is family, isn’t she? She wouldn’t…” Clara trailed off, her hands twisting nervously. Eleanor felt the familiar hum of a new lead sparking through her mind. Between Marianne’s vague answers, her presence near the study earlier in the day, and now news of this heated argument, the pieces began to suggest a deeper resentment between the niece and her uncle. “Thank you, Clara,” Eleanor said finally, though her tone left Clara visibly uneasy, as if sharing the truth had only made the situation more dangerous.

Eleanor’s thoughts churned as she pieced together Clara’s revelation. She made her way to the study again, the place seeming heavier each time she entered. The silence in the room was deafening, and Victor’s slumped body cast a long shadow over her investigation. Her eyes returned to the letter opener buried in his chest, its ornate handle glinting under the light. She thought back to Marianne’s trembling hands, Harold’s resentment, Clara’s fear, and Richard’s mocking defiance. Each had a reason to lash out—but Eleanor needed something tangible. 

Her gaze fell to the desk again, her mind returning to the strange empty rectangular imprint in the dust. She leaned closer this time, examining the edges as if the blank space itself would reveal its secret. Suddenly, her attention snapped to the ashtray beside it. Several ashes were scattered across the desk, but something was off—most of the cigars in Victor’s study were full-bodied, perfectly rolled imports from Havana. Yet within the ashtray, Eleanor spotted a different type of residue—crumbled, dry paper mixed with the ashes. Someone had burned something. 

Eleanor carefully picked through the faint remains, finding tiny blackened fragments that refused to disintegrate. She inhaled sharply as she realized what she held—a sliver of red wax, faintly stamped with a crest. It must have been part of a sealed letter or document. Whatever had been burned, it was important—important enough that someone wanted it to vanish. But who? And more importantly, what connection did it have to Victor’s murder? This discovery felt heavy with implications and yet maddeningly incomplete.

Eleanor carefully slid the ashtray closer, her gloved fingers running over the edge as though it might whisper the secret of what had been destroyed. The wax fragment was familiar, though she couldn’t immediately place it, and that only heightened her frustration. She tucked it carefully into an evidence bag, her mind already leaping to what such a document might have meant to Victor—and to his killer. Her thoughts were interrupted by the sound of hushed voices filtering through the hallway. She strode out of the study and found Marianne and Harold standing in the dim light of the foyer, their heads close, their words sharp but muted. 

As soon as they spotted Eleanor, they stiffened and stepped apart, Harold’s face twisting into his practiced calm while Marianne’s lips pressed into a thin line. “Trouble in paradise?” Eleanor asked, her eyes darting between them. Marianne opened her mouth to respond, but Harold cut her off. “We were just... clearing a misunderstanding,” he said smoothly, though his tension betrayed him. Eleanor glanced to Marianne, whose narrowed eyes looked like they wanted to speak volumes, but instead, she crossed her arms. “Go ahead, Harold,” Marianne spat, her voice carrying an edge. “Tell her your version. You seem awfully good at rewriting stories tonight.”

Harold shot her a warning look, but it only deepened Eleanor’s curiosity. “You both seem to have a lot weighing on you,” Eleanor said, her tone deliberate. “Maybe one of you would like to explain what’s really going on between you?” After a loaded pause, Harold finally exhaled through his nose and turned on his heel, disappearing back into the sitting room without another word. Marianne remained, her hands trembling again, but when Eleanor stepped closer, she tightened her posture. “He’s nothing but a snake,” Marianne muttered, almost to herself, avoiding Eleanor’s gaze. “If anyone had cause to kill Uncle Victor, it was him.” The venom in her voice was palpable, but Eleanor only narrowed her eyes. Marianne was pointing fingers again—too quickly, too easily. The deflection was growing harder to ignore.

Eleanor watched Marianne retreat down the hall, her footsteps quick and agitated, before turning her attention back to the study one more time. The sense of something missing—the burning of the document, the strange fragmented clues—gnawed at her. Victor’s desk was enormous, with drawers that had yet to be fully examined. She began opening them systematically, moving past neatly ordered ledgers, correspondence, and legal paperwork. Then, in the bottom drawer, tucked beneath a stack of outdated files, she found something far more intriguing: a handwritten letter. The penmanship was scrawled and uneven, not Victor’s confident hand, but the urgency bled through every stroke. 

*Victor,* it read, *I’ve done as you asked, but this game is getting dangerous. Richard is growing suspicious, and I can’t keep this quiet much longer. If you don’t provide what you promised soon, I’ll have no choice but to protect myself. The consequences are on you.* 

Eleanor’s breath caught. The letter wasn’t signed, but the tone was clear—someone had been involved in a scheme with Victor, one that had spiraled out of control. The mention of Richard’s name felt almost too convenient now, given his behavior and Clara’s earlier accusation. But the letter lacked something—a key detail, a date, a name connecting it to someone other than vague insinuations. Eleanor stared at it longer, memorizing its structure before tucking it into another evidence bag. A deal gone wrong, secrets spilling into betrayal—and yet Eleanor couldn’t shake the feeling that she still didn’t know the full depth of Victor’s enemies. The circle was tightening, but the final knot hadn’t yet revealed itself.

Eleanor exited the study and made her way down the hall, her mind humming with possibilities. Victor’s life had been full of deals, debts, and dangers—it seemed as though everyone in the mansion had a motive for wanting him silenced. But the burning question stuck like a thorn: who was desperate enough to strike with that level of precision? 

She found Richard near the rear of the house, this time pacing under the low beams of the servants’ quarters. His usual nonchalance had slipped; he looked agitated, his fists clenching and unclenching as though trying to strangle invisible memories. Without preamble, Eleanor stepped into his line of sight. “Tell me the truth, Richard,” she said sharply, pulling out the letter she’d just found. “What was Victor holding over you? What had you so suspicious?” 

Richard froze, eyes darting briefly to the paper before meeting Eleanor’s hard stare. For the first time, the swagger dimmed from his voice. “That bastard…” he muttered under his breath, shaking his head. “He enjoyed playing with people’s lives. Always the king on his little chessboard.” When Eleanor stayed silent, he exhaled heavily, as if surrendering a piece of himself. “Victor knew something about me. Something from a long time ago. He said if I ever crossed him, if I ever left this house, he’d ruin me. Ruin everything I’ve built.” His jaw tightened. “But that’s all you’ll get from me. Whatever game he was playing in the end, I wasn’t part of it.” 

“And yet Clara says she saw you near the back door around the time of the murder,” Eleanor countered, watching his expression closely. Richard hesitated for the briefest of moments, and then his lips curled into a sneer. “Clara’s a frightened little rabbit—she’d say anything to save herself if she thought it’d help. Maybe you should look more closely at her, Detective.” With that, he pushed past Eleanor, brushing her shoulder with a deliberate force that left her standing in the dim hall, his words echoing strangely in her ears.

Eleanor stayed rooted in the hallway, Richard's sneer replaying in her mind. His defensiveness was expected—but the veiled jab at Clara unsettled her. She’d assumed Clara was nothing more than a frightened assistant overwhelmed by the murder's chaos, yet Richard had planted a seed of doubt that now refused to stay buried. Deciding to press the matter, Eleanor found Clara standing in front of the large window in the sitting room, staring out into the rain-soaked garden. Her reflection in the glass was pale, her features pinched with worry. 

“Miss Finch,” Eleanor began softly, stepping into the room. Clara turned, startled, her arms hugging herself tightly. “Richard seems to think you have something to hide,” Eleanor continued, her tone firm but not unkind. “Why would he say that about you?” 

Clara shook her head almost violently. “He’s lying! He’s trying to deflect suspicion away from himself, can’t you see that? He—he hated Mr. Pembroke!” Her voice broke, and her face crumpled with tears. “I’d never hurt anyone. I was loyal to Mr. Pembroke. I worked for him for years.” 

Eleanor stepped closer, her eyes narrowing slightly. “You say you were loyal, but perhaps not to the end. What were you so frightened of when you found his body? You hesitated earlier when describing your actions. Did you move something? Take something?” The questions hit like stones, making Clara falter. 

Her lips trembled, but then she whispered, “No… I didn’t take anything. I swear. But when I saw him…” Her voice dropped lower, her words more hesitant. “The room wasn’t empty. I think I heard someone leave. But they were fast—so fast I thought I imagined it at first.” 

“Who?” Eleanor pressed urgently, taking a step closer. 

“I-I don’t know,” Clara stammered. “It—it could have been anyone.” Her tears spilled fresh, but Eleanor wasn’t sure now if they were tears of fear—or guilt.

Eleanor left Clara in the sitting room, her sobs still echoing faintly as the detective’s mind turned over the revelation. Someone had been in that study when Victor was killed, slipping out just as Clara stumbled upon the body. Clara’s breakdown seemed genuine—but genuine fear or a desperate act of manipulation was yet unclear. The rain outside had intensified, lashing against the mansion’s tall windows as Eleanor walked back into the foyer, where she found Marianne once again. This time, the young woman was seated on the grand staircase, her head cradled in her hands, her shoulders shaking slightly. 

Eleanor stopped just short, waiting for her to notice the presence of another. Slowly, Marianne lifted her head, her dark, piercing eyes locking onto Eleanor’s. There was no pretense of grief on her face anymore—only anger. “Have you found what you’re looking for yet, Detective?” Marianne asked bitterly. “Or are you just enjoying tearing all of us apart?” 

Eleanor knelt slightly to meet her at eye level, her voice cool. “I’m here to find the truth, whether you like it or not. Speaking of which, you’ve given me vague answers all day. If you have nothing to hide, then tell me—what is *your* truth, Marianne? If you hated Victor so much, why stay here under his roof, even after he tried to control every part of your life?” 

Marianne’s expression faltered, her lips pressing into a thin, trembling line. “Because… because I didn’t have a choice,” she admitted quietly. “He held all the strings. Everything I had was because of him. But that doesn’t mean I killed him.” She paused, her voice shaking. “Do you think I didn’t know what he was doing to the others? Screwing Richard over, keeping Clara so dependent on him she couldn’t leave, dangling whatever Harold wanted just out of reach? Victor thrived on control. He kept us all trapped in his little web.” Her eyes burned as fresh tears threatened to spill. “But someone finally broke free, didn’t they?” Eleanor studied her carefully. Marianne’s anger felt righteous, but there was something in her anguish that whispered of guilt. “You’re right about one thing,” Eleanor said coolly, standing once more. “Someone did. The question is who.”

As the storm outside raged on, Eleanor retreated to the quiet of the library, her head spinning with the tangled web Victor Pembroke had created around himself. Each suspect—Marianne, Harold, Richard, Clara—had a motive, a reason to resent Victor’s suffocating control. But her mind kept circling back to the fragment of burned wax, the missing document, and the desperation hidden in the letter she had found. Someone had tried to erase part of the story, but why? And what had Victor been protecting so fiercely? 

Flipping through the notebooks and ledgers she had collected from Victor’s study, Eleanor’s sharp eyes caught a familiar crest scribbled in the corner of one page. Her stomach tightened as the image aligned with the burned red wax—her earlier suspicion confirmed. It was a family crest, one that matched the Pembroke insignia engraved above the mansion’s grand entrance. It must have belonged to something tied directly to the Pembroke name, Eleanor realized—something deeply personal to Victor. She scanned the page and found a single cryptic note scribbled in the margin: *“Insurance. Marianne must never know.”* 

Eleanor’s breath hitched. Insurance? Insurance for what? The mention of Marianne was telling—it was as if Victor himself was pointing from beyond the grave. If Marianne wasn’t supposed to know, that meant the burned letter, or whatever the missing piece had been, must have concerned her directly. Eleanor stood, her pulse quickening. Something had snapped that night; someone had acted, desperate to bury a truth that threatened to undo them. And yet, despite the mounting evidence pointing toward Marianne, Eleanor’s instincts pulled in another direction—a darker, quieter corner of the house.

Eleanor’s instincts led her to the dimly lit servant’s corridor where Richard had slunk off earlier. The stifling silence of the narrow hallway was broken only by the soft patter of rain against the nearby windows. She pushed open the door to the tool shed at the far end, where Richard often claimed to be when questioned. The damp air was thick with the scent of soil and rust, and Eleanor’s boots scraped against the gritty floor as she entered. A row of tools hung neatly along the wall, each one marked by decades of wear—except for a small spade lying haphazardly on the workbench, its surface wiped unnaturally clean.

She moved closer, narrowing her gaze as she noticed faint smudges along the edge of the spade’s handle. Blood, barely visible, as if smeared in haste. Her heartbeat quickened. Richard hadn’t been as careful as he thought.

Eleanor straightened, letting her breath steady. If Richard had used the spade—and from the evidence, he likely had—it didn’t match the murder weapon. The letter opener had killed Victor, precise and deliberate, but this spade... This was something else. Misdirection? An attempt to conceal something before or after the murder? She felt the swell of possibility rising as her eyes scanned the shed’s dim corners, looking for anything amiss. It was then that her hand brushed against a nearby work apron hanging limp against the wall. She froze as her fingers closed around a crumpled scrap of paper stuffed hastily into its pocket.

Unfolding it carefully, Eleanor’s pulse raced as the message came into view: *“Meet me tonight, 10 p.m., the study. We’ll settle this before it goes any further.”* It was unsigned, but the handwriting was unmistakably Victor’s. Eleanor felt the pieces sliding together—someone had been summoned to the study that night, and Victor had been expecting tension, perhaps even conflict. But the note revealed something more: premeditation. And whoever had come to "settle this" had left Victor dead.

Clutching the note, Eleanor strode back into the mansion, her steps deliberate as her suspicions began to crystallize. The storm outside howled, rattling the windows, but it was the brewing storm within the house that filled the air with unease. She called everyone to gather in the sitting room—Marianne, Harold, Richard, and Clara. They entered one by one, their expressions guarded, nerves laid bare beneath the overhead chandelier’s harsh light. The house seemed to hold its breath as Eleanor stood before them, the note and evidence bags in hand.

“I believe I’ve uncovered the truth,” Eleanor began, her voice steady, cutting through the tension. “Victor Pembroke’s killer is in this room.” Clara gasped softly, her hands flying to her mouth, while Harold’s jaw ticked with tension. Richard leaned back against the wall, arms crossed, more curious than alarmed, and Marianne, seated stiffly on the edge of an armchair, stared darkly at the detective, her expression unreadable. 

“To understand why Victor died,” Eleanor continued, “we have to piece together the web of control he cast over everyone here. He manipulated you, forced secrets out of you, and hurt you in ways unimaginably intimate. Each of you had a reason to want him gone. But tonight wasn’t just about blame. This murder was about desperation, someone protecting something—or someone—they couldn’t afford to lose.”

She strode to the center of the room, holding up the crumpled note. “Victor called someone here tonight. He wanted to ‘settle this,’ as he wrote. But the meeting went sideways, and now he’s dead.” She gazed at them all, letting her silence stretch before landing her sharp eyes on Clara. “Miss Finch. You were the one who found the body. You heard people moving. You pointed fingers at everyone else. But you never told me the full truth about what you were hiding that night, did you?” 

Clara turned pale, her trembling hands clutching at each other as all eyes settled on her. “I didn’t—what are you saying?” she stammered, on the verge of tears. But Eleanor didn’t flinch, her words hitting like a hammer. “Victor had a document—a letter, a truth he thought he could use to control you. And when he threatened to expose it during your meeting that night, you panicked. Didn't you, Clara?”

Clara’s composure crumbled entirely, her knees buckling until she collapsed onto the armchair behind her. Tears streamed down her face as her thin voice broke the thick silence. “He left me no choice!” she cried, her words spilling out like floodwaters. “Victor… he knew everything about me, about the debt I’d hidden—things that could ruin my life. He was going to use them against me, to keep me under his thumb forever. I begged him to stop, but he just laughed, said he owned me. That’s when I… I saw the letter opener on the desk...”

The room grew deathly silent, the others frozen in various states of shock. Marianne leaned forward, her eyes wide and disbelieving, while Harold muttered a quiet, stunned curse under his breath. Richard, ever the brooding observer, only shook his head with an almost bitter satisfaction. 

Clara continued, trembling violently now. “I didn’t mean to! I didn’t even… I didn’t plan it! It just… happened.” Her voice dropped lower, barely a whisper. “Afterwards, I panicked. I burned the document he was threatening me with before anyone could see it. I thought... I thought maybe if I made enough noise, it would seem like someone else—” She choked on her words, burying her face in her hands. “But I can still see him, slumped there, and I’ll never forget it.”

Eleanor remained still, letting Clara’s confession fill the room like a heavy fog. The detective’s instincts had been right—Clara wasn’t just a frightened bystander; she was a woman who had snapped beneath the weight of Victor’s cruel manipulations. Finally, Eleanor spoke, her tone calm but unyielding. “You made a choice, Clara. You can try to justify it, but it won’t change what happened.” She stepped toward the shattered assistant, her shadow stretching long against the firelight. “Victor Pembroke controlled lives, manipulated fears—but in the end, his cruelty created the very thing that destroyed him. And now, it’s over.”

As officers arrived to take Clara away, Eleanor stood in the doorway, watching the others silently process the truth. The mansion, built on dominance and secrets, seemed almost to exhale with relief. Justice, Eleanor thought grimly, was rarely clean or satisfying—but it was, at least, the truth. And tonight, the truth had finally been unearthed.

Closing the book with a snap, she decided to check the study one more time, hoping for anything she might have overlooked. Clara jumped at the question, spinning around to face her. “I—I just... I thought maybe I could help,” she stammered, wringing her hands. “There’s nothing you can do for him now,” Eleanor said bluntly, watching Clara’s reaction. Her face crumpled, and tears began to spill down her cheeks. “He didn’t deserve this,” she mumbled. “And whoever did this... they deserve to be caught.” There was something overly insistent in her tone, a desperation that made Eleanor pause. She glanced once more at the letter opener, wondering at Clara’s apparent fixation on it. “You seem awfully distressed about a man you claim was hard to work for,” Eleanor prodded. Clara froze, her red-rimmed eyes wide, but before she could respond, there was a loud crash from somewhere upstairs, followed by hurried footsteps echoing down the hallway. Both women turned sharply toward the sound. “What the hell was that?” Clara whispered, her voice barely audible. Eleanor didn’t answer—she was already moving.

As Harold disappeared down the hall, Eleanor stepped back into the foyer, where Clara was nervously wringing her hands near the grand staircase. Richard, leaning against the far wall, watched her with his usual unsettling calm. “Odd fellow, that Harold,” Richard drawled, a crooked smirk tugging at the corner of his mouth. “Always scheming for a way to one-up old Victor. Couldn’t stop talking about that damn property he wanted.” Eleanor moved closer, her sharp eyes fixed on him. “And what about you, Richard? Victor seemed particularly concerned about *you* in his notes. ‘God help me if Richard learns the truth,’ he wrote. What truth would that be?” Richard’s smirk vanished in an instant, his jaw locking tight. “Victor liked to talk in riddles. Always made you feel like he knew some dark secret about you, even if he didn’t,” he muttered, the edge in his tone unmistakable. “If he wrote that, it was just his way of keeping me on a leash.” “And yet here you are, standing under the same roof as a man you clearly despised,” Eleanor pressed, studying his reaction. Richard’s dark eyes flicked to Clara, who was watching from a distance, then back to the detective. “I’ve got nothing to hide, Detective,” he said, his voice flat but defensive. “But I’d keep an eye on her if I were you. The little mouse isn’t as harmless as she looks.” He nodded toward Clara, who turned visibly pale at his words but remained silent.

Eleanor allowed Harold to leave, but his warning lingered in her mind like a distant rumble of thunder. She returned to the foyer, where Clara was now pacing nervously near the grand staircase. “Miss Finch,” Eleanor called, and Clara froze, her hands wringing together. “A moment, please.” The assistant approached hesitantly, her gaze darting toward the study as if afraid some ghost might emerge. “You’ve worked for Mr. Pembroke for a while, haven’t you?” Eleanor asked, clasping the notebook tightly. Clara nodded. “Five years. He trusted me with everything—at least, I thought he did.” Her voice wavered, carrying a note of sorrow. "Did he ever tell you about being threatened or feeling unsafe?" Eleanor pressed. Clara hesitated, then shook her head. “Not directly, but... he always seemed paranoid lately. Locking doors behind him, snapping at anyone who asked too many questions. And...” She trailed off, visibly struggling over whether to continue. “And what?” Eleanor urged. Clara’s face grew ashen. “I saw him arguing with Richard yesterday. It wasn’t just tense—it was ugly. Mr. Pembroke was furious about something, and Richard stormed off. I... I don’t know what it was about, but Victor told me to stay out of it.” Eleanor filed this away, her instincts sharpening. Richard’s hostility seemed ever more potent, but she couldn’t shake the feeling that something deeper was at play. Clara fidgeted anxiously, her voice dropping to a whisper. “Please, Detective, don’t tell Richard I said anything. He... he frightens me.”

As Harold disappeared down the hall, Eleanor stood still for a moment, her mind calculating. She pocketed the notebook and made her way back to the foyer, where Clara was now nervously wringing her hands near the grand staircase. “Miss Finch,” Eleanor called, and Clara jumped as though caught doing something wrong. “I need you to tell me exactly what you saw when you found Victor’s body.” Clara swallowed hard, glancing nervously at the study door. “I had gone to deliver a stack of papers he asked for earlier… but when I knocked, he didn’t answer. The door was unlocked, so I pushed it open, and that’s when I saw him, slumped over the desk with… with the letter opener.” Her voice cracked at the memory. “I screamed. I didn’t mean to, but it just… I ran out and called the police.” Eleanor studied Clara’s trembling form. “Did anyone else come into the study before the police arrived?” Clara hesitated, her eyes darting toward the staircase. “I… I don’t think so. I can’t be sure. I wasn’t paying attention.” Eleanor frowned, sensing there was more Clara wasn’t saying. “You’re certain the door was unlocked when you entered?” Clara nodded quickly. “Yes, I swear! But Mr. Pembroke never left it unlocked unless he—unless someone else was with him earlier.” The statement hung in the air like a shadow, and Eleanor stored the detail away. “I’ll need you to stay close,” she instructed firmly, though her gaze briefly flitted toward the staircase Clara kept glancing at, wondering what, or who, might still be lurking.

Descending the stairs once again, Eleanor caught sight of Richard Lyle standing by the grand bay window, his silhouette sharply outlined against the rain-streaked glass. He was lighting a cigarette, his movements slow and deliberate. The deep orange glow briefly illuminated his face, which bore an expression as stormy as the night outside. “You’re not too unsettled by all of this, are you, Mr. Lyle?” Eleanor said as she approached, her tone laced with intrigue. Richard exhaled a curl of smoke before answering. “Unsettled? No. People like Victor Pembroke tend to attract trouble. It was only a matter of time, really.” Eleanor leaned against the nearby wall, observing him. “You keep saying things like that—how he deserved what came to him. Some might take it as more than just commentary.” Richard smirked, turning his head to face her. “And yet I imagine you’re more interested in asking those fancy types upstairs where they were tonight. It’s always harder for people like them to keep their hands clean.” His words carried an edge, a bitterness. “You seem particularly focused on Marianne,” Eleanor pointed out. Richard’s smirk grew colder. “She plays the part of the dutiful niece, but she’s not as innocent as she looks, Detective. Take it from someone who’s had to clean up her messes before.” Eleanor tilted her head, intrigued. “Messy enough to risk Victor’s wrath?” Richard dropped the cigarette stub into the empty vase on the window ledge, his expression hardening. “Let’s just say she’s got skeletons of her own. Ask her about the inheritance.” His words were a low growl, delivered like a challenge, before he pushed past Eleanor and walked off into the darkened hall. She watched him go, his presence leaving behind more questions than answers.

Eleanor descended the stairs slowly, her thoughts churning. The cigar, the hesitation in Marianne’s answers, the ominous notes in Victor’s journal—nothing fit neatly, yet the tension in the house was thick enough to slice. As she reached the bottom step, the sound of raised voices drew her attention. From the kitchen at the far end of the hall, Richard Lyle’s deep, gravelly tones clashed with Harold Gaines’ indignant baritone. “You always had your nose in his business, Harold,” Richard was growling as Eleanor approached, staying just out of sight. “What did you expect to happen? He was bound to push back eventually.” Harold’s voice sharpened with fury. “Don’t try to twist this on me, Lyle. You’re the one skulking around the house at all hours. God only knows what you’ve done in his name!” “Watch your damn mouth,” Richard warned, and there was a sound of something heavy slamming—a fist on the table, perhaps. Eleanor decided it was time to intervene. She stepped into the room and immediately felt the tension swell. Richard leaned lazily against the counter, his muscles taut despite his casual posture, while Harold stood stiff and glaring, his tie slightly loosened. "Trouble in paradise?" Eleanor quipped, her tone biting. Neither man replied immediately, but Harold finally spat, “Ask him what he was doing in the west gardens tonight.” Richard’s eyes flicked toward Harold, narrowing in defiance. “Planting nightshade, apparently,” he sneered. Eleanor raised an eyebrow at the cryptic exchange. “Enough,” she said coolly. “Both of you—sit. I want to know exactly what this argument is about, and where the hell the two of you were when Victor was killed.”

Eleanor lingered outside Marianne’s door for a moment, her mind churning. Something about the way Marianne had reacted—the defensive tone, the vague timeline—only deepened the detective’s doubts. But before Eleanor could dwell further, she heard faint footsteps echoing from the far end of the hallway. Turning sharply, she spotted Richard Lyle, the groundskeeper, slipping into a room at the very end of the left wing. His movements were swift and deliberate, but his attempt to go unnoticed only made him more suspicious. Intrigued, Eleanor followed, her footsteps silent against the carpet. She came to what appeared to be a small storage room and peeked through the slightly open door. Inside, Richard was rifling through a stack of papers on an old writing desk, his back to her. “Looking for something, Mr. Lyle?” Eleanor asked, stepping inside. Richard spun around, his eyes narrowing sharply, though he quickly masked his expression with a neutral scowl. “Just cleaning up,” he grunted. “This whole place is falling apart, Detective. Thought I’d make myself useful while you dig for secrets.” Eleanor’s gaze dropped to his hands, which were clutching a yellowed envelope. “Useful, or opportunistic?” she countered, nodding toward the envelope. Richard hesitated, then shoved it into his coat pocket. “You think you’re clever, don’t you?” he said with a sneer. “I don’t have to talk to you.” Eleanor stepped closer, her voice low. “You weren’t in this part of the house earlier. What brought you here now, Richard? What are you hiding?” Richard stared at her for a moment before brushing past her roughly, muttering, “I’m not the one with something to hide in this cursed house,” as he fled down the hallway, leaving Eleanor with more questions than answers.

Eleanor descended the staircase, her thoughts swirling with contradictions. The cigar stub in Marianne’s room, the cryptic entry in Victor’s notebook, and the tensions between the suspects—all pieces of the puzzle were jagged and without clear edges. As she reached the bottom of the stairs, Richard Lyle was leaning against the frame of the front door, his coat on and a cigarette between his lips. “You’ve been scurrying around like a mouse, Detective,” he said with a smirk, exhaling smoke into the humid night air. Eleanor didn’t rise to his bait. “Going somewhere, Mr. Lyle?” she asked coolly. He tapped his cigarette against the doorframe, scattering ashes onto the threshold. “Work’s done for the day, isn’t it? Nothing keeps me here now.” She stepped closer, eyeing him carefully. “The man who hired you lies dead, and you think you can simply walk away?” Richard chuckled low in his throat, shaking his head. “Hired me? No, he tolerated me. There’s a difference. Victor wasn’t the sentimental type, you know. Kept me around because I’d seen too much to let me go and live peacefully somewhere else.” He dragged on the cigarette before flicking it onto the damp driveway. “Did you see too much tonight, Mr. Lyle?” Eleanor asked sharply, her voice like a whip. Richard’s smirk faltered, and for a moment, there was something unreadable in his eyes. “I saw nothing I want to talk about,” he muttered, pulling the door open and stepping into the cold night. Eleanor watched his retreating figure, feeling the weight of unspoken truths trailing him like smoke in the fog.

Eleanor descended the staircase, her mind tangled in the growing web of clues. As she reached the base, she noticed Richard Lyle skulking near the back entrance to the kitchen, as though trying to avoid her. His shadowed figure paused when he saw her approach, his expression unreadable in the dim light of the corridor. “Richard,” she called, her voice firm, “you seem to have a habit of lurking in the dark. Care to explain where you’ve been tonight?” Richard smirked faintly, leaning against the doorway with his arms crossed. “You’re the detective—you tell me.” Eleanor didn’t flinch at his sarcasm, instead stepping closer, folding her arms to match his stance. “Victor’s journal says he feared you learning the truth,” she stated pointedly, watching his reaction. Richard’s smirk faltered but didn’t fully disappear. “Victor was paranoid. He saw ghosts in every corner. What exactly is it you think he was hiding from me?” Eleanor tilted her head. “That’s what I’m trying to figure out. But I can’t help noticing how you seem awfully calm for someone under suspicion of murder.” Richard’s eyes darkened, his voice low. “Calm is what you learn when you’ve spent your life cleaning up after people like Victor. He thought his money made him untouchable. Maybe he finally touched the wrong nerve with someone. But it wasn’t me, Detective.” The words hung between them, bitter and sharp, as Richard slipped through the door leading into the dark garden. Eleanor let out a slow exhale, her instincts pulling her in all directions but unwilling to let him slink too far from her scrutiny.

Descending the stairs once more, Eleanor’s mind spun as she tried to piece together the fragments of motive and opportunity hovering over each suspect. As her boots touched the hardwood of the foyer again, Richard Lyle leaned casually against the wall near the grand clock, his dark eyes tracking her movements like a predator watching prey. “Find something interesting snooping around upstairs, Detective?” he asked, a wolfish grin tugging at the corner of his mouth. Eleanor crossed her arms and met his gaze with steady calm. “You seem awfully relaxed while the rest of the house trembles, Mr. Lyle. Care to explain that confidence?” Richard chuckled, his voice a low rumble. “Unlike some people here, I don’t have anything to hide.” His calm demeanor only served to make Eleanor more cautious. “And where were you during the time of the murder?” she asked pointedly. Without hesitation, Richard replied, “Out back in the garden. You can check my gloves in the shed if you don’t believe me—they’re still covered in soil.” He leaned in slightly, his voice dropping. “But you don’t seem too interested in those types of details, now, do you? You’re heading for the wrong target. I told you before—Marianne’s the one you should watch. She’s playing innocent, but she’s got more backbone than she lets on. Uncle Victor probably crossed the line with her once too often.” He grinned again, almost enjoying the drama. Eleanor said nothing, filing his words away. She knew better than to let his swagger steer her too fully. She finally broke his gaze and turned toward the study yet again. Something didn’t add up, and it was beginning to smell deliberate.

Leaving the study, Eleanor stepped through a side hallway that led toward the back entrance Clara had mentioned. The house stretched long and claustrophobic in this wing, shadows pooling in the neglected corners. She pushed open the heavy door that led to the garden, stepping out into the wet chill of the night air. The garden itself sprawled in wild tangles, though the freshly turned soil in one of the beds suggested Richard’s presence earlier. Yet something else caught her eye. Just to the side of the garden path, partially smothered by leaves and mud, was a muddy footprint—a sharp, narrow sole. It was too clean-edged to belong to Richard’s heavy, worn boots. Crouching for a better look, Eleanor noted its size and shape: feminine, likely from a small heeled shoe. Her mind immediately snapped to Marianne, remembering the sharp click her heels made on the polished floors earlier that evening. But then, a soft rustling in the bushes pulled Eleanor from her thoughts. She rose carefully, her hand instinctively moving toward her coat pocket, where her flashlight rested. Someone, or something, was nearby. “Who’s there?” she called sharply. The rustling ceased, replaced by an eerie silence. After a moment, Richard Lyle rounded the corner, his dark frame illuminated just barely by the weak outdoor lanterns. His face had that same smirk, but there was a wariness to his stance now. “Taking a midnight stroll, Detective?” he asked, voice dripping with mockery. “Funny, I thought I was the one they accused of creeping around at night.” Eleanor caught the glint of something metallic near his waist—pruning shears, she realized, confirming his claim about gardening. But the footprint behind her didn’t match him, and she knew better than to be baited by his sly tone. “I don’t suppose you noticed anyone else out here tonight, did you?” she asked coolly. Richard shrugged, his grin widening. “Maybe. Maybe not. But what’s a little suspense in a murder mystery, eh?” He walked past her, hands in his pockets, whistling a low, casual tune as he headed back toward the house.

Eleanor stepped out of the study, her thoughts swirling, and made her way toward the back entrance. The narrow hallway leading to it was poorly lit, the dark wood paneling seeming to absorb the dim light. She pushed open the heavy back door, its creak echoing in the stillness of the night. Outside, the rain had slowed to a drizzle, and the garden stretched before her in shadowy rows. Squinting against the faint moonlight, her eyes caught a faint disturbance in the soil near the edge of the garden, where the soft earth seemed unevenly packed. Kneeling down, she ran her hand over it and uncovered a small fragment of parchment partially buried in the dirt. It was torn, damp, but legible enough to read a scrawled name: *Marianne Pembroke.* Eleanor’s pulse quickened as she turned it over. The rest of the paper was too soaked to reveal more, but the placement felt deliberate, as though someone had discarded it—or hidden it—in haste. Rising to her feet, she froze as she heard the crunch of footsteps behind her. “Looking for something?” Richard’s gravelly voice cut through the stillness, and she turned sharply to find him standing in the garden path, his large frame illuminated faintly by the weak outdoor bulb. He had a cigarette dangling from his lips, his hands thrust into his coat pockets. “You seem to spend a lot of time snooping around dark corners, Mr. Lyle,” Eleanor shot back, tucking the fragment into her pocket. He exhaled a plume of smoke, watching her with lazy amusement. “And you seem to enjoy assuming the worst. Shouldn’t you be interrogating Marianne, considering how her name’s showing up in places it shouldn’t?” His smirk deepened, but Eleanor noted the flicker of tension in his jaw. Whether it was from keeping secrets or something more, she couldn’t yet tell. “Don’t wander off too far,” she said coolly, brushing past him toward the house. Richard’s low chuckle followed her, but it sounded less confident than before.

Eleanor left the study, her thoughts clouded by Clara’s timid accusation. As she moved toward the kitchen, where the back entrance connected to the house, a metallic clattering caught her ear. Peering into the room, she found Harold standing at the sink, rinsing a glass. He turned when he heard her enter, his face taut with irritation. “Can’t a man get a moment to breathe without you tailing him, Detective?” he asked, setting the glass down with a loud clink. “I wasn’t aware the kitchen was your sanctuary, Mr. Gaines,” Eleanor replied dryly, stepping closer. Her eyes drifted to his hands, gripping the counter tightly, and her voice dropped to a more probing tone. “Why don’t you tell me where *you* were just before Victor’s body was discovered?” Harold clenched his jaw, clearly biting back a retort before answering. “I was in the drawing room, going over some documents Victor had been stalling to sign—ones related to that blasted land deal we discussed earlier.” Eleanor raised an eyebrow. “And you were alone?” The pause before he replied was short but noticeable. “Yes, alone. Victor wasn’t exactly the hospitable type tonight, so there was no house tour or socializing happening.” Eleanor noted the hostility laced through his words, her instincts sensing something deeper. “Strange,” she said softly, “I’ve heard conflicting accounts about who was where tonight. One of you must be lying, and the truth does have a habit of leaking out—often when it’s least convenient.” Harold’s eye twitched at her remark, but he stiffened his posture. “Maybe you should stop chasing your tail and focus on the obvious,” he snapped. “Victor had no shortage of enemies, but his niece? You’d be a fool not to take a closer look at her.” His deflection wasn’t lost on Eleanor as she silently decided it was time to visit the back entrance for herself.

Eleanor left the study and made her way toward the back entrance Clara had mentioned. The heavy oak door creaked faintly as she pushed it open, stepping out into the damp night air. The garden stretched ahead, shrouded in mist from the earlier rain. She held her flashlight steady, scanning for any signs of disturbance, when her beam landed on muddy footprints leading away from the door. They were fresh, distinct, and far too large to belong to Clara or Marianne. Following the trail carefully, Eleanor’s pulse quickened as the tracks led her toward the garden shed Richard had claimed to be working in. The door was slightly ajar, and she could hear the faint scratching of something inside. Pushing the door open, she found Richard leaning nonchalantly against the potting bench, cleaning his gardening shears. His boots, caked in mud, sat near the edge of the bench, exactly as he said they would be. “Detective,” he greeted, not looking up. “Can’t sleep without poking around, can you?” Eleanor ignored his taunt, shining the flashlight toward him. “Clara claims she saw someone near the back entrance after the murder. Care to explain?” Richard paused, his fingers tightening briefly around the shears before he set them down. “I already told you where I was. Believe me or don’t.” His tone was defiant, but Eleanor noticed the tension in his shoulders—subtle but telling. “Funny,” she said coolly, “because those footprints outside match your boots.” Richard folded his arms and tilted his head, a smirk tugging at his lips. “Sure they do. Must be the work of an honest gardener, then. Or are you going to arrest me for walking too loudly?” His casual deflection only deepened Eleanor’s unease. She stepped closer, meeting his gaze in the dim light of the shed. “One slip’s all it takes, Mr. Lyle,” she warned. “And I’ll be there when you make it.” For the first time, his smirk faded, replaced by a brief flicker of something darker.

Eleanor left the study, Clara’s whispered accusation echoing in her ears. As she stepped into the hallway, she found herself face to face with Harold Gaines once more, his expression taut with the kind of unease that comes from eavesdropping. “Interesting theory she’s spinning in there, isn’t it?” Harold said coolly, crossing his arms. Eleanor wasn’t surprised that he had overheard; he had a knack for appearing at just the right—or wrong—moment. “I wouldn’t consider theories too seriously until I’ve got evidence to back them up,” she replied evenly, trying to gauge his intentions. Harold smirked faintly, though his jaw was tight. “Well, if you’re looking for motives, Detective, you might want to dig into Victor’s financials. He wasn’t exactly as solvent as he let on, you know. Got a little desperate in his old age.” Eleanor frowned, unsure whether this was an attempt to deflect suspicion or to weaponize another clue. “Is that information from a ‘business partner’ or a rival?” she asked pointedly, her tone sharpening. Harold shrugged, his veneer of mild indifference cracking just slightly. “Take it however you like,” he said. “I only know what I know. And if you’re looking for someone with something to gain, you might want to ask Clara how much Victor paid her to keep her secrets. He wasn’t just kind enough to hire her out of pity.” He tilted his head meaningfully, then turned and walked off, leaving Eleanor with more questions than answers, her suspicions swirling like storm clouds.

Leaving the study once more, Eleanor sought out Richard in the hopes of confronting him about Clara’s claim. She found him outside the back entrance, leaning against the cold, ivy-covered stone wall with a cigarette burning lazily between his fingers. The thick scent of smoke and wet earth hung in the air. “Detective,” he greeted, exhaling a plume of smoke that seemed to swirl with his words. “Come to accuse me of something else?” Eleanor crossed her arms. “Clara says she saw someone near this door right after she discovered Victor’s body. She thinks it was you. Care to explain?” Richard chuckled, a sound both low and menacing. “Clara?” he repeated, dragging out her name with disdain. “She’s always worked herself into a frenzy over nothing. Probably imagined it. I already told you where I was—out in the garden, not skulking around some back door.” Eleanor’s gaze never wavered. “Garden work at night? Convenient.” He shrugged, unbothered. “Plants don’t wait for perfect timing, Detective.” As his grin widened, her eyes were drawn to something peculiar—an unmistakable smudge of dirt on the edge of the back doorknob. Fresh dirt, damp and dark. “What’s that then, Richard?” she asked, pointing toward it. His expression faltered ever so briefly before he snuffed out his cigarette against the wall. “I went through that door earlier in the evening,” he admitted, though no trace of guilt colored his tone. “Had to grab a tool from the shed. What are you implying exactly?” Eleanor held her silence, growing ever more aware of how easily suspicion could align against Richard. But the timing gnawed at her, as did the ease with which he explained it away. Nothing about this man seemed straightforward—except, perhaps, how suspicious he wanted to appear.

Eleanor decided it was time to speak with Harold again, her suspicions sharpening in light of Marianne's revelation. She found him in the dining room, standing by the window and staring into the darkness outside, his silhouette framed by the heavy green drapes. His expression was unreadable as she approached, but the tightness in his jaw betrayed that he was anticipating her. “Marianne tells me you had a rather heated argument with Victor earlier,” Eleanor said without preamble. Harold turned slowly, his face carefully composed. “I wouldn’t call it ‘heated,’” he replied evenly. “It was a disagreement. Business-related, as most of our discussions were.” Eleanor stepped further into the room, studying his every movement. “She said Victor accused you of betrayal. Sounded personal to me.” For a brief instant, a crack appeared in Harold’s calm demeanor—his lips parted slightly, his nostrils flared—but he quickly collected himself. “Victor liked to dramatize everything,” he said dismissively. “He was upset because I challenged one of his decisions. That’s hardly betrayal.” Eleanor moved closer, lowering her voice. “Did you threaten him, Harold?” At this, Harold’s shoulders stiffened visibly. “Threaten him?” he repeated, his voice rising indignantly. “No. It’s not my fault Victor made enemies out of everyone around him. He loved playing the victim whenever someone challenged his authority.” His eyes narrowed slightly. “I wonder… have you stopped to think who benefits most from Victor’s death? Because it isn’t me. Marianne stands to inherit everything now, doesn’t she?” His deflection was smooth, but not seamless. Eleanor didn’t miss the underlying fury in his voice, nor the way his hand lingered near the edge of the curtain, gripping it so tightly it threatened to tear. She walked away without responding, her doubts multiplying with each passing minute.

Eleanor found Harold in the dining room, staring out at the rain-streaked windows with a glass of whiskey in his hand. He turned when he heard her footsteps, his brows knitting together as he set the glass down on a nearby table. “Detective,” he said tersely, the sharp edge of patience running thin in his voice. “This whole situation is absurd. I have nothing to hide, and yet I feel like I’m on trial.” Eleanor approached him slowly, her expression unreadable. “Marianne claims she overheard an argument between you and Victor earlier,” she began, watching for any flicker of reaction. “Something about betrayal and trust. Care to elaborate?” Harold’s jaw tightened, but he kept his composure. “Our disagreements were strictly business. Yes, there was tension lately. Victor was stalling on a deal we’d been negotiating for years. We argued, like we often did—but I’d hardly call that motive for murder.” His voice grew colder. “Marianne always did enjoy eavesdropping. She probably heard what she wanted to hear.” Eleanor studied him for a long moment, noting how he didn’t deny the encounter. “What was the deal really about, Harold? You’ve been awfully vague.” Harold hesitated, then sighed as if the weight of the question pulled it from him. “It was a property dispute, alright? A piece of land Victor owned that I’ve been after—a lot of money was riding on it. But Victor… he didn’t trust anyone. He thought everyone was after something.” Harold grimaced, more irritated than remorseful. “Still, he had no right to throw that word around—‘betrayal.’” Eleanor caught the slight tremor in his voice on that last word, and her sharp instincts pricked. “He used it often, then?” she asked softly. Harold snapped his head toward her, his face darkening. “Not often. But when he did, it usually meant someone close to him disappointed him.” There was a finality to his words, as if he’d slammed a door Eleanor was about to push through.

Eleanor decided it was time to confront Harold again, her patience with his polished demeanor wearing thin. She found him nursing a drink in the parlor, his back to the door as he gazed into the crackling fire. The amber liquid in his glass caught the light as he swirled it absentmindedly. “Settling in comfortably for someone whose business partner is dead,” Eleanor remarked as she entered, her voice cutting through the quiet. Harold didn’t flinch, though his grip on the glass tightened ever so slightly. “A drink helps steady the nerves, Detective,” he replied smoothly, turning to face her with a faint smile that didn’t reach his eyes. “Is that what you told Victor earlier? Perhaps before you stormed out of his study?” Eleanor shot back, her tone sharp. Harold’s smile faltered, but only for a moment. “Marianne’s been whispering in your ear, hasn’t she?” He set the glass down on the mantel. “Yes, Victor and I had an argument. It wasn’t the first, and it won’t be the last argument I’ve had in my career—though this one, of course, ended more definitively.” His attempt at dark humor fell flat under Eleanor’s glare. “What was the argument about?” she pressed. Harold hesitated, his jaw tightening. “Victor was being unreasonable about a piece of land I was trying to buy from him. He accused me of… unethical tactics. It got heated, I admit, but when I left him, he was in one piece. I don’t kill over business disputes, Detective. That’s not my style.” Eleanor stepped closer, studying him as if she could peer past his practiced mask. “Convenient words, Mr. Gaines, but Victor clearly didn’t trust you anymore. That much is evident.” Harold's eyes flickered with something unreadable, but his calm control returned as quickly as it had slipped. “You’ll find no blood on my hands, Detective,” he said firmly, his voice steady. Eleanor couldn’t decide whether his confidence was reassuring or chilling.

Eleanor processed Marianne’s revelations, though she’d begun to suspect every word spoken tonight was laced with half-truths and misdirection. She found Harold sitting stiffly in one of the velvet armchairs in the sitting room, a glass of whiskey untouched in his hand as he stared into the unlit fireplace. His face was a picture of grim tension, his usual composure cracking at the edges. “Mr. Gaines,” Eleanor began, stepping inside. “It seems someone overheard you and Victor having a heated discussion earlier. An argument about trust and money, perhaps?” Harold’s head snapped up abruptly, his jaw tightening. “Marianne told you that, didn’t she?” His voice had cooled to a brittle edge, sharp and defensive. “She’s got a wild imagination, Detective. Victor and I had a disagreement, yes, but we’ve had them before. Business *disagreements,* nothing more.” Eleanor circled him slowly, her tone measured. “Disagreements that would make you storm out of the study? What was so important that it raised your temper tonight of all nights?” Harold shot to his feet, setting the whiskey glass down hard enough that the fragile crystal rattled. “Victor owed me,” he snapped, his polished demeanor momentarily slipping. “He owed me for years of loyalty, for pulling his ventures out of the mud every time they faltered. And yet, every chance he got, he’d pull the rug out from under me. Isn’t that enough?” Eleanor stared at him for a long moment, her instincts whirring. “At the moment, Mr. Gaines, I’m not sure whose word is enough.” Harold sat back down heavily, but the bitter anger still burned behind his eyes.

Eleanor found Harold in the sitting room, nursing a glass of whiskey that trembled faintly in his hand. His usually composed demeanor had frayed; tension carved lines across his face as he stared into the amber liquid, lost in thought. "Mr. Gaines," Eleanor announced, stepping into the room, her voice slicing through his reverie. I left that study alive, and so was he.” Eleanor watched as his hand drifted back to the glass of whiskey, his grip firm but trembling slightly.
