Eleanor found Harold in the sitting room, seated stiffly in a leather armchair with a glass of brandy in hand. He didn’t look up as she entered, instead swirling the amber liquid absentmindedly, lost in thought. “You and Victor argued earlier today,” Eleanor stated bluntly, watching him closely. Harold’s grip on the glass tightened, but he didn’t deny it. “Yes, we argued,” he admitted, his voice low and measured. He finally raised his eyes to meet hers, a flicker of resentment sparking behind them. “Victor had a way of pushing people’s limits. He was impossible to negotiate with.” Eleanor stepped closer, her boots clicking softly against the hardwood. “What were you negotiating, exactly? Marianne said she overheard you two—something about trust and money.” Harold’s jaw tightened, and he set the glass down on the side table with more force than necessary. “It was business,” he snapped. “Victor owed me—owed a lot of people, frankly—but he refused to honor his commitments. For someone so wealthy, he was a stingy old bastard. He thought he was untouchable.” Harold rubbed his temples as if the memory alone pained him. “I told him I wouldn’t tolerate it anymore. I left to cool off. And now he's dead.” Eleanor tilted her head. “Convenient timing, isn’t it?” Harold shot her a sharp look, his composure cracking an inch. “If you think I killed him, you’re mistaken. He was alive when I left, Detective. I might’ve wanted my due, but I’m not a murderer.” His words sounded rehearsed, too calculated to be entirely natural. Eleanor let the silence stretch, the weight of his defensiveness thick in the room. Finally, she turned away, but not before noting the faint trace of sweat glistening on Harold’s brow.

Eleanor left Harold to stew in his defensiveness and headed back through the dim halls of the sprawling Windsor mansion, feeling the heavy press of its secrets in the walls around her. Passing the library, she noticed something she hadn’t before: a faint line of muddy footprints trailing in from the back of the house, leading toward a side door that appeared slightly ajar. The prints looked fresh and smeared, as though someone had tried to cover their tracks. She crouched down to inspect them more closely and caught a faint streak of red mixed into one of the prints—a smudge of what looked disturbingly like blood. The trail abruptly stopped before the library door, which was shut. Eleanor slowly turned the knob and stepped inside. The room was dark, save for the muted glow of a fire crackling in the ornate hearth. Richard Lyle sat in one of the wingback chairs near the fireplace, his long legs stretched out lazily, a book resting unopened in his lap. Startled by Eleanor’s unexpected entry, he straightened, his eyes narrowing. 

“Can’t a man read in peace?” he grumbled, but Eleanor ignored the remark. Her sharp eyes flitted to his boots propped near the fire, caked with damp mud and faint streaks of something darker along the edges. Eleanor nodded toward them. “Interesting choice of footwear for garden work. Looks like you’ve been walking somewhere a bit messier than dirt.” Richard sat up with a slow, deliberate movement, his lips curling into a sly grin. “Careful there, Detective. You’re starting to sound like you’ve already made up your mind.” Ignoring his deflection, Eleanor stepped closer, her gaze unwavering. “Those footprints stop right outside this door, Richard. Care to explain why?” Richard shrugged, leaning back in his chair with maddening composure. “I might’ve taken a shortcut through here earlier. But blood on my boots? Seems like you’re grasping at ghosts. Maybe you should look somewhere else for your killer.” His words were delivered with casual arrogance, but his fingers fidgeted slightly, giving away a crack in his veneer. Eleanor didn’t reply, but she mentally flagged both Richard’s trail and his nerves. Whatever game he was playing, he was playing it extremely well.

Eleanor left Harold to stew in his frustration and headed toward the kitchen, where Clara was nervously scrubbing an already clean countertop. The clattering of dishes masked her shallow, uneven breaths. “Miss Finch, we seem to keep circling back to you,” Eleanor said, her voice slicing through the tense air. Clara froze, gripping the edge of the counter. “I’ve told you everything I know,” she insisted, her tone laced with desperation. “Perhaps,” Eleanor replied, stepping closer. “But you’ve been awfully jumpy for someone who claims they’re innocent.” Clara turned to face her, her cheeks flushed. “Of course I’m jumpy! I found my employer murdered. You can’t possibly understand what that feels like!” Eleanor studied her carefully, noting the way her fingers fidgeted with the cuff of her sleeve. “I noticed you were quick to name Richard earlier,” Eleanor said. “Why? Is it personal?” Clara’s face turned an even deeper crimson. “Richard’s always been trouble. Everyone knows it. He hated Mr. Pembroke—he made no attempt to hide it.” She tightened her arms around herself before adding, almost in a whisper, “And he had a key to the back door. He’s the only one who did.” Eleanor’s interest piqued. “A key to the back door?” she repeated. Clara nodded. “I saw him use it before, when he wasn’t supposed to. Mr. Pembroke gave him too much trust.” Her words hung in the air like bait, and Eleanor couldn’t ignore the slight satisfaction that flickered in Clara’s eyes as she spoke. It was as though Clara wanted her theory to stick, to firmly shift the lens of suspicion. Eleanor narrowed her gaze, wondering whether Clara's fear was real—or a carefully woven performance.

As Eleanor left Harold to simmer in his strained composure, she found Clara once again lingering by the base of the grand staircase, wringing her hands nervously. The young assistant looked jittery, her gaze flickering toward Eleanor as if waiting to be called upon. Sensing unease, Eleanor approached her directly. “Clara, you’ve been here long enough to know Victor’s habits. Did he ever mention anything about these ‘debts’ Harold claims he owed?” Clara hesitated, her face flushed. “I—he didn’t tell me much, but I know he was… protective of his money.” She looked down at her feet, her voice almost trembling. “Sometimes he’d even ask me to shred certain letters, ones he didn’t want anyone else to see. I never asked questions. It wasn’t my place.” Eleanor raised an eyebrow, leaning in slightly. “Letters? Like the one I found crumpled in his hand tonight? You knew what was written on it.” Clara’s eyes widened, panic flashing across her features. “No! I swear, I didn’t know anything about that letter. But…” She trailed off, biting her lip. “But I had a bad feeling,” she finished quietly, as though ashamed of the confession. “Victor hadn’t been himself these past few weeks—like he was distracted. Anxious. He locked the study door more than usual, and he started keeping people at arm’s length.” Eleanor frowned, filing the observation away. “And yet you entered an unlocked study tonight to find him dead,” she said pointedly, her tone pushing Clara just a little harder. The assistant’s hands flew to her chest defensively. “You can’t think I… no! I—I’ve only ever done as I was told—” She cut herself off abruptly, as though realizing how her excuses might sound. Eleanor’s expression hardened. “I’m not making accusations yet, Clara. But in this house, it seems everyone has a bad feeling—and I’m starting to understand why.”

The storm outside raged harder, wind howling through the cracks of the old mansion as Eleanor paced the dim hallway near the study. Something was gnawing at her, a detail she couldn’t yet place. She reached into her pocket and retrieved the fragment of paper she had found clenched in Victor’s hand, reading the scrawled words again: *"…cannot protect you any longer."* The handwriting was jagged and uneven, almost frantic. Eleanor approached her, her sharp eyes scanning Clara’s pale face. “You’ve been acting nervous all night, Clara,” she said quietly but firmly. “If there’s something you haven’t told me, now is the time.” Clara froze, the clinking of the teacups betraying her shaking hands. “I—no, I told you everything,” she stammered, avoiding Eleanor’s penetrating gaze. But Eleanor leaned in closer, lowering her voice. “Victor was protecting someone. Could it have been you?” Clara’s head snapped up, her eyes wide with terror. “No! Eleanor moved to the dining room, where the long table, covered in a green velvet runner, stood as empty and untouched as the rest of the cavernous mansion. Her eyes darted toward where she’d last seen him in the hall but found only shadows. “I... I told you, it was dark. I’m not sure of anything. He’s just so... threatening. You seem afraid of more than just Richard.” Clara’s lower lip quivered, and then, almost involuntarily, she whispered, “Harold. As Eleanor left Harold to stew in his own tension, she found Clara hovering anxiously near the base of the staircase, her eyes darting nervously between Eleanor and the study door down the hall. “Detective,” Clara began, her voice hesitant, “I… I think there’s something else I should tell you.” Eleanor stopped mid-step, crossing her arms and fixing Clara with a steady gaze. “Go on.” The young assistant hesitated, chewing her lip as she glanced around to confirm no one else was within earshot. “Mr. Pembroke and Harold weren’t the only ones fighting,” she said quietly. “Earlier today, Mr. Pembroke and Miss Marianne had a terrible row. The house felt heavier as the night deepened, its grand hallways cloaked in shadows that seemed to mirror the secrets Eleanor was chasing. Eleanor’s thoughts were interrupted by a soft creak behind her. I hope you’re finding what you’re looking for.” Eleanor held up the cigar. “This. Eleanor sought out Marianne again, her earlier suspicions now taking clearer shape. She found her standing near the dining room window, staring out at the storm battering the darkened estate grounds. Eleanor stopped in front of her, forcing Marianne to meet her gaze. “So you didn’t argue? Eleanor’s thoughts churned as she absorbed Clara’s revelation, but before she could act on it, she noticed Richard walking back inside through the back entrance, shaking rainwater from his coat. Even I have my limits,” he said, his voice smooth but with that ever-present edge of mockery. She approached him, studying his face, his posture, his calculated ease. “Clara claims she saw someone near the back door around the time of the murder,” she said, her tone hard and direct. “She thinks it was you. Then, with a sly grin, he replied, “Did she now? Just that she seems... jumpy. More than usual, don’t you think?” His words, like everything else he said, felt like bait—but Eleanor couldn’t deny the spike of doubt they planted. Richard seemed content to stoke fires wherever he could, spreading doubt as if it were sport. But was he deflecting... or was he confident because he knew she was looking in the wrong direction?

Driven by this new revelation, Eleanor sought Marianne again, expecting resistance. She found her in the parlor, perched on the edge of a faded velvet chaise like a restless bird, her fingers clutching a teacup that rattled faintly in its saucer. Marianne looked up as Eleanor entered, her eyes wary but defiant. “Detective,” she said coolly, setting the cup down. “Have you come to interrogate me further?” Eleanor ignored the jab and stepped closer. “I spoke with Clara. Something about him threatening to cut you off if you left?” Marianne’s eyes darkened, her expression tightening. “Clara needs to learn to mind her own business," she muttered. Then, after a pause, she straightened her spine, locking eyes with Eleanor. "Yes, we argued. I’ve been telling Uncle Victor for *months* that I want to move to London, start a life of my own. But no, he thought he could dictate everything. That’s how he always was—controlling, manipulative. Marianne clenched her jaw, a flicker of something unreadable crossing her face. “I would’ve left eventually, Detective. I’d leave. That would’ve hurt him more than anything.” Eleanor didn’t respond immediately, the weight of Marianne’s words stirring more questions than answers.

Eleanor decided it was time to revisit Marianne, whose alibi grew thinner with every revelation. She found her in the dimly lit conservatory, sitting by the rain-streaked glass, staring out at the tangled garden outside. The gloomy room suited Marianne’s mood—she looked restless, her fingers twitching as they toyed with the hem of her sleeve. “Marianne,” Eleanor said, her voice cutting through the silence like a knife, “Clara overheard your argument with Victor earlier. Care to explain what that was about?” Marianne flinched but quickly composed herself, her jaw tightening. “It wasn’t important,” she replied coolly, refusing to meet Eleanor’s eyes. “It sounded important enough,” Eleanor said, stepping closer. “You wanted to leave, didn’t you? And your uncle refused. He threatened to cut you off.” Marianne glared at her now, her dark eyes flashing with something between anger and despair. “Does it matter? Yes, I wanted to leave. I hated it here, hated the way he hovered over me like some kind of puppet master. But that doesn’t mean I killed him.” Eleanor held her gaze, unrelenting. “You stormed out of the study after that fight. Where did you go?” Marianne hesitated, the faintest crack of panic creeping into her expression. “To my room,” she said, but her voice lacked conviction. “Did anyone see you there?” Eleanor pressed, her words knife-sharp. Marianne’s silence spoke louder than any answer might have. The detective straightened, letting the weight of the pause settle. “You had motive, Marianne, and you were unaccounted for during the time of the murder. If there’s something you’re not telling me, now’s the time.” Marianne’s fists clenched in her lap, but she remained silent, staring back at Eleanor with a fierce, unreadable defiance that left the detective more suspicious than ever.

Eleanor’s thoughts churned as she pieced together Clara’s revelation. She made her way to the study again, the place seeming heavier each time she entered. The silence in the room was deafening, and Victor’s slumped body cast a long shadow over her investigation. Her eyes returned to the letter opener buried in his chest, its ornate handle glinting under the light. She thought back to Marianne’s trembling hands, Harold’s resentment, Clara’s fear, and Richard’s mocking defiance. Each had a reason to lash out—but Eleanor needed something tangible. 

Her gaze fell to the desk again, her mind returning to the strange empty rectangular imprint in the dust. She leaned closer this time, examining the edges as if the blank space itself would reveal its secret. Suddenly, her attention snapped to the ashtray beside it. Several ashes were scattered across the desk, but something was off—most of the cigars in Victor’s study were full-bodied, perfectly rolled imports from Havana. Eleanor carefully picked through the faint remains, finding tiny blackened fragments that refused to disintegrate. Whatever had been burned, it was important—important enough that someone wanted it to vanish. But who? And more importantly, what connection did it have to Victor’s murder? This discovery felt heavy with implications and yet maddeningly incomplete.

Eleanor stepped back from the desk, the weight of the burned fragment lingering in her fingers. It was clear now—someone had destroyed evidence, but not carefully enough. They had been rushed or careless, leaving enough traces to pique her suspicion. Her thoughts turned to Victor’s ominous journal entry: *“Betrayed trust. Impatience. God help me if Richard learns the truth.”* She pocketed the wax fragment and prepared to leave the room when she spotted a faint scrape along the floor beneath the desk. Kneeling, Eleanor ran her fingers over the marks—a chair had recently been dragged back, sharply and unevenly, as if someone had stormed away from the desk in rage or haste. As she stood, the study door creaked open behind her. Turning, she found Marianne in the doorway, her silhouette tense against the light from the hallway. “Why are you still in here?” Marianne asked, her tone edged with annoyance, though her voice wavered slightly. Eleanor noticed her hands were once again trembling, fingers gripping the edge of the doorframe as though to steady herself. 

“Just uncovering what someone desperately wanted to hide,” Eleanor said, watching Marianne’s reaction closely. Marianne flinched slightly, her dark eyes shifting towards the desk and then back to Eleanor. “You think I know something, don’t you?” she whispered bitterly. “You’ve already decided I’m guilty.” Eleanor stepped toward her, keeping her voice calm but firm. “What I’m deciding is that everyone in this house is lying about something—including you. So why don't you tell me why burning evidence was necessary?” 

Marianne’s face twisted, her controlled demeanor faltering. “I don’t know what you’re talking about. I’ve done nothing wrong,” she snapped, but her words came too fast, too defensive. Without waiting for a response, she turned and walked briskly out of the study, her heels clicking angrily against the hallway floor. Eleanor stood alone once more, her suspicions of Marianne deepening, but the truth remained just out of reach, entangled in secrets and half-truths.

Eleanor pocketed the fragment of wax and exited the study, her mind racing with theories. Stepping into the dimly lit hallway, she paused, listening. The mansion was unnervingly quiet, save for the faint ticking of the grandfather clock in the foyer. She moved toward the wing where the bedrooms were located, her boots muffled by the plush carpet. As she passed Harold’s room, she noticed the door was closed but not completely latched. A faint rustling sound came from within. Hesitating for only a moment, Eleanor pushed the door open just enough to see inside.

Harold was standing near his wardrobe, his back to the door. He didn’t notice her at first, too absorbed in his task. Eleanor’s sharp eyes caught the glint of metal as he placed something inside a leather satchel. “Planning a trip, Mr. Gaines?” Eleanor asked coolly, stepping inside without waiting for an invitation. Harold flinched, spinning around with wide eyes, but he quickly recovered, his features hardening into irritation. “No, Detective, just organizing some things to keep my mind off this nightmare,” he replied, zipping the bag shut hastily and placing it on the floor. 

Eleanor crossed her arms, leaning casually against the doorframe. “What are you hiding in there?” she asked, her tone laced with challenge. Harold’s nostrils flared, but he forced a steely smile. “Nothing of concern to you. Just personal documents.” Eleanor’s gaze dropped to the satchel, lingering there deliberately. “Funny—seems like someone’s been destroying documents in the study,” she said smoothly. Harold’s face twitched, a flash of something unreadable crossing his features before he quickly shook his head. “Not me,” he said curtly. “Victor’s affairs were his disaster, not mine.” But his tone was defensive, and Eleanor didn’t miss how his posture subtly shifted, as though he were shielding the bag.

Eleanor exited the study with the burned fragments tucked carefully into a small evidence bag. The weight of its implications pushed her to move faster, her steps echoing ominously through the dim hall as she approached Clara again. The assistant startled when Eleanor appeared, as though caught in the act of some unseen guilt. “Clara,” Eleanor began, her voice low and direct, “do you know anything about Victor burning a document earlier today? Perhaps something sealed in red wax?” Clara’s eyes widened, her face blanching almost instantly. “I… no—I mean, not exactly,” she stammered. Her fidgeting hands betrayed her as she avoided Eleanor’s penetrating stare. “Not *exactly*?” Eleanor pressed, stepping closer. The air grew heavier between them. 

Clara hesitated again, desperate to steady her quivering voice. “Victor did... destroy things sometimes. Letters, contracts he no longer cared about, things like that. Whatever was burned in that study—and whatever Clara knew—it was another piece of the tangled web Eleanor was slowly unraveling.

Eleanor exited the study with the charred fragment of wax turning over in her gloved fingers, her mind racing. The crest was faint, but it appeared to be a Pembroke family seal—likely something Victor had kept private. Someone had destroyed the document deliberately, but why? Eleanor studied her for a moment, her sharp observational instincts combing over every detail: the tightly drawn lines of Marianne’s lips, the stiffness in her posture. “I don’t stop poking until the truth starts making sense, and right now, it doesn’t,” Eleanor replied. Marianne exhaled sharply, breaking the stifling silence left behind. Richard rose to leave without a word, his expression unreadable, while Harold poured himself another glass of brandy, his hands oddly still now that the chaos had a name. Eleanor stayed behind, standing in the center of the room as the storm outside began to fade. The truth had come to light, but like all murders born of desperation, it left nothing behind but emptiness—emptiness in the rooms Victor Pembroke had once ruled and in the souls of the people who had survived him.

Clara’s trembling turned into outright shaking as her defense crumbled under Eleanor’s accusation. Tears streamed down her face, yet her silence screamed louder than words. The room grew unbearably tense, the storm outside seeming to echo the chaos within. All eyes bored into Clara, but Eleanor wasn’t finished.

“No,” Eleanor said suddenly, her sharp gaze swinging away from Clara. “That’s what you wanted me to believe, wasn’t it?” The room froze, the shift in Eleanor’s tone chilling. Her gaze landed on Richard, who still leaned against the wall, his smug expression gone, replaced by something colder—calculating. “You’ve been hiding behind deflection all night, Richard. Richard’s jaw clenched, his hands dropping to his sides, fingers curling into fists. Eleanor pressed on. “Victor used his power over everyone here, but with you, he went too far. Precise.” Richard’s dark eyes bore into hers, but he stayed silent. Still, his silence was deafening. 

Eleanor stepped forward, her voice a blade. “You left through the back door to clean yourself up, relying on Clara’s panic to muddy the timeline and blame. But it all comes back to you, Richard. The letter, the spade, the fresh dirt... you were panicking, trying to clean up the mess you made after the murder.”

Richard exhaled slowly, a low, humorless laugh escaping his lips. “Should’ve shoved that spade deeper in the shed,” he muttered, his voice resigned. His shoulders sagged, his false calm unraveling completely as two officers stepped from the shadows of the room, positioned there by Eleanor as insurance. “Fine, Detective. You got me,” Richard said, spreading his hands mockingly as the officers approached. “You know as well as I do—Victor had it coming.” His voice darkened with bitter finality, but Eleanor stayed stone-faced.

As they hauled him out into the storm, the room remained silent, heavy with the weight of unspoken truths. Marianne, Harold, and Clara—all still prisoners to the ghosts of Victor Pembroke’s manipulations—watched Richard disappear into the night. Eleanor lingered a moment longer, glancing at the rain-streaked window before turning her back on the house of secrets. Justice had been served—or at least, what little justice could come from the tangled wreckage of Victor Pembroke’s life.

Clara’s composure crumbled entirely, her knees buckling until she collapsed onto the armchair behind her.
